_hand_authored: Hand-mapped against public/hero/base-photo.png. UNLIKE hero-scene.json (generated by scripts/render-base-scene.mjs from a real camera) this plate is an AI-generated photograph with no camera to project from, so every number here was measured off the image with scripts/hero-grid.mjs and checked against a real composite via /hero-check + scripts/hero-shot.mjs. Edit it by hand, re-shoot, and look at the result — several of these corners were wrong by 2-4% on the first pass and only the composite showed it.
_geometry_note: Coordinates are PERCENTAGES of the plate (0-100), x rightward, y downward. lib/hero-regions.ts divides by 100 to reach the 0-1 fractions the compositor works in. Percentages because that is the unit the mapping grid prints, and hand-editing 41.4 is less error-prone than 0.414. Quads are topLeft, topRight, bottomRight, bottomLeft in TEXTURE order (corner i of the quad is corner i of the texture).

faces._alcove_edges: Top edge measured along the soffit line at ZOOM=14: y=7.0 at x=22, 7.6 at x=26, 8.0 at x=29, 8.9 at x=36, 9.3 at x=39, 9.6 at x=42 — it FALLS to the right at about 0.13% per 1% of x. Bottom edge (wall meets pan) measured at ZOOM=8: y=85.0 at x=26, 84.5 at x=32, 84.0 at x=38, 83.4 at x=42, a fall of about 0.10% per 1% of x.
faces._alcove_corners: Found by scanning horizontal luminance profiles across the alcove rather than by eye, because an interior corner between two matte planes is a gradient minimum, not a hard edge. INTERIOR CORNER: darkest column sits at x=23.56% at y=12/20/30 and 23.69% at y=40/60 — near vertical, leaning 0.2% right over the wall's height. Left of it the profile falls steeply (174 at x=17.5 down to 131 at x=24) which is the return raking away from the light; right of it the profile is flat at ~132 across to x=42, which is the back wall facing us. ALCOVE RIGHT EDGE: darkest column at x=42.54% (y=12) to 42.67% (y=20-78). The previous single-plane region ran to 43.2 and overhung onto the bright partition face beyond it. OUTER LEFT EDGE of the return is the luminance PEAK at x=17.5% — a convex corner catching light, where the return meets the room wall.
faces._alcove_scale: Real kit dimensions, and the reason these two planes are separate regions rather than one warped sheet. Back wall 60in over a measured 19.05% of plate width; left return 32in over 6.1%. That is 0.317%/in against 0.191%/in — the return is foreshortened to 60% of the back wall's scale, so a single quad spanning both cannot tile a 24in panel correctly on either. Panel height 94.5in maps to the wall's full measured height. At 24in panels: the back wall is 2.5 panels, giving seams at 40% and 80% across it; the return is 1-1/3 panels, giving one seam. The return's quad is deliberately ordered CORNER-FIRST (topLeft is the interior corner, not the outer edge) so tiling starts at the corner and a full panel terminates there, which is how the kit actually installs — the offcut lands at the outer edge where it is least visible.
faces._panel_top_derivation: The panel top is a PERSPECTIVE-LEVEL line at the top of the alcove — deliberately not the plate's soffit, and deliberately not the product's honest 94.5in either. Both were tried. Following the soffit read crooked, because the plate's soffit genuinely IS crooked: it falls 2.5% left-to-right where true perspective for a level line on this camera is 1.1%, an artifact of how the plate was generated. Stopping at 94.5in was geometrically honest but left a band of bare wall above the panels and stranded the plate's baked-in shower head (about 100in above the pan) floating on it. DEPARTURE FROM SCALE, ON PURPOSE: the field now renders about 103.2in against a real 94.5in panel, because this plate's alcove measures roughly 105in pan-to-soffit and full-height is the look that reads right — to be resolved by the next plate, not by tilting this line. METHOD: the same solve as before. With a level camera screen y is linear in real height, so every horizontal line on a plane is the pan line scaled away from the horizon by a constant. Horizon y=36.45 from the pan's own two edges; camera 65.9in above the pan from the back wall's 60in width. Anchored at the soffit's LOWEST point, the right corner, set to y=9.90 rather than the measured 9.68 so antialiasing cannot poke above it. That fixes the factor at -0.5660 and gives y_top = 36.45 + (y_pan - 36.45) * -0.5660 per plane, applied to each plane's own pan line so all three tops meet exactly at both corners. VERIFIED below the measured soffit at every x: clearance 1.62% at the interior corner, 1.22 at x=29, 0.93 at 33, 0.71 at 36, 0.49 at 39, 0.27 at 42, 0.22 at the right corner. The wedge of bare plate that leaves at the left — 1.6% tapering to nothing at the right — is expected and reads as the soffit's own reveal.
faces._left_return_top_note: The return's top does NOT stop at a level line, and it does not follow a ceiling either — because there is no ceiling above it to follow. MEASURED: vertical luminance columns at x=20.5, 21.0, 21.5, 22.0, 22.5, 23.0 and 23.4 all brighten monotonically downward from y=0 to y=12 with no step anywhere (150->191, 143->189, 130->180, 119->172, 105->151, 90->129, 78->114); the strongest downward gradient in any of them is +5, i.e. noise. What LOOKS like a ceiling line running down to the corner is the corner's own ambient occlusion: each column darkens sharply as x approaches the corner while every column brightens with y, so the iso-luminance contours run diagonally and read as an edge. They are not an edge. The wall simply runs off the top of the frame. So the panels do too: the outer end is set to y=-17.0, off frame, and the canvas clips it. What remains visible is the edge descending from about (21.5, 0) to the corner, which is the slope of that shading contour and therefore agrees with the plate. The corner vertex is shared with showerWallBack at exactly (23.56, 8.82) — one point, no step. The back wall's line could NOT be re-anchored to meet a higher return: it is already anchored at its tightest soffit constraint (0.22% clearance at the right corner), and raising the corner end to 7.40 would put it 1.2% ABOVE the soffit at x=42. heightIn stays 103.2 to match the other planes, which is the field height AT THE CORNER; at the outer edge the field spans about 137in of the return's own scale. That is not a rectangle in the world, and it is the honest consequence of following a shading contour instead of a ceiling that this plate does not have.
faces._right_return_note: The third wall. Measured by fine luminance profile across x=42.0-45.5: the strip is a bright band (171.4 average against the back wall's 163.8 — it faces the window) bounded on the left by the back wall's corner at 42.65 and on the right by a hard dark line at x=44.00, constant at every height sampled. It is only 1.35% of plate width for 32in of real depth, so its scale is 0.042%/in against the back wall's 0.317% — roughly a seventh, which is what near-edge-on looks like. Its base drops steeply as it approaches the camera (83.2 at x=42.85, 85.3 at 43.2, 88.8 at 43.6); the bottom-right is set to 90.0 rather than the extrapolated 91.4 because under-reaching leaves a sliver of plate and over-reaching paints panel onto the pan. Quad is ordered CORNER-FIRST like the left return, so the panel terminates at the interior corner. At this compression its single seam (32in over 24in panels) lands around x=43.6 and is all but invisible, which is correct — you would not see a joint on a wall viewed this close to edge-on.
faces._counter_ends: Measured at ZOOM=16 on both ends: the wood band starts at x=47.0 (a hard vertical edge, wall to its left) and stops at x=71.0. It was previously carried as 45.9-69.8, so the material started on bare wall and stopped a full 1.2% short of the counter's right end — both ends the user circled.
faces._backsplash_note: A band of the same material standing on the counter's back edge and running up the wall. Height is derived, not measured off the plate — the plate has no splash to measure. The vanity reads 36in to the counter top over 33% of image height at this depth, i.e. 0.917% per inch, so a 4in splash is 3.7% and a 6in splash 5.5%; the compositor scales the band from the vanity's own backsplash selection.
faces._backsplash_right_end: The splash stops at x=65.7, NOT at the counter's right end at x=71.0. There is a wall corner at x=65.0 (y=5) leaning to 65.6 (y=48) — visible as a break in the ceiling line above and confirmed by the wall tone changing across it — and a splash runs along a wall, so it ends where the wall turns. The counter itself is unaffected and still runs the full 47.0 to 71.0. The consequence is deliberate and visible: roughly 5% of plate width of bare wall sits above the counter's right end.

_clip_note: Where a texture is ALLOWED to land, as against the quad which says how it warps. This plate has no rendered ID mask (the Three.js scene had one), so occlusion is hand-traced instead. First polygon of each list is the outer boundary; a polygon nested inside another punches a hole, via the even-odd fill rule. A HOLE MUST LIE ENTIRELY INSIDE ITS OUTER POLYGON — even-odd counts crossings, so any part of a hole that pokes out the other side flips back to filled and paints where nothing should. That is why the plant cut-out below stops just short of the wall's bottom edge instead of running past it. Traced deliberately tight: under-covering leaves a sliver of plate showing, which reads as shadow; over-covering smears material across a plant or a toilet, which reads as broken.
_plant_note: The plant cut-out in backWall is the one place a polygon is the wrong tool. A fern has no outline, so this is a compromise between two visible failures: too tight and wall material paints stripes across the leaves, too loose and a grey wedge of bare plate opens up beside them. It is tuned to hug the dense core and let the sparse outer fronds take a little bleed, because bleed on a few leaf tips reads as shadow while the grey wedge reads as a hole. A per-pixel mask keyed off the foliage's green would beat this outright and is the obvious next step if it ever needs to be better.
_clip_simplification: These used to carry notches cut around the plants, the toilet and the plant pots. They don't any more: public/hero/base-photo-occlusion.png restores every foreground object over the finished composite in one pass, so a clip only has to describe the SURFACE now, not what happens to be standing on it. Where a boundary still bends, it is following real geometry — the vanity toe kick, the partition base, the shower curb — not an obstacle.
_seams_note: Ambient occlusion the compositor paints along a corner AFTER the materials land. The plate already carries its own corner darkening and multiply passes that straight through, so these are deliberately WEAKER than the plate's own: measured, the interior corner dips from shoulders of ~171 to 151 at the darkest column, a 12% drop over roughly 2% of plate width each side. Painting that again on top would double it, so `strength` is set near half the measured depth — enough to keep the joint reading once a dark panel texture has flattened the plate's own gradient, not enough to draw a black stripe. `from`/`to` are the corner's endpoints and `halfWidthPct` the fade distance either side, both in plate percent.

vanityLeft._measured: Hard dark line at x=49.5 between wall and cabinet face.

vanityRight._measured: Cabinet right edge at x=77.45, dark line to 77.6.

panWallLeft._measured: Pan meeting the alcove walls along its back edge.

vanityToe._measured: Toe recess: cabinet face ends 87.3 at x=50, 85.8 at x=70; floor begins 90.

_fixture_note: Tight boxes around the plate's baked-in matte-black fixtures, for recolouring them to the dealer's selected finish. Given as [x, y, w, h] in plate percentages. A box may be drawn a little wider than the fixture it covers, which usually costs nothing: the tint only touches pixels below a luminosity threshold, so wall, counter and cast shadows inside a box are left alone. Sized off the same measurements as the anchors below. The vanity light is deliberately absent — it is decor in the plate, not a product the dealer picks, and recolouring it would imply otherwise.
_fixture_faucet_note: The lavatory faucet is two boxes, not one, because a full-width box spanning the spout's height also spans the hard shadow line under the mirror frame at y=48.5 — 44 of 49 pixels across that row sit below the cutoff, so the whole line recoloured and the vanity grew a gold stripe above the tap. The spout gets its own narrow box through that band; the wide box picks up below it, where the handles are and the mirror's shadow is not.
_fixture_head_note: The back-wall head region is GONE. The plate's baked-in head and its cast shadow are now painted out by plateRepairs before anything composites, and a modelled head is drawn on the LEFT return instead — see modeledHead. Leaving a tint box on the back wall would recolour a fixture that is no longer there.
_anchor_note: The anchors below are used only by the Three.js fallback plate; the photo plate recolours the baked-in fixtures above instead of pinning product photographs. They are kept because that fallback still pins photos, and because the measurements are the record of where the plate's fixtures actually are. The plate has matte-black fixtures baked in. A product photo is pinned OVER each one and has to cover it outright, because multiply can darken the black blob but can never erase it. unitPerIn is therefore sized from the measured pixel footprint of the baked-in fixture, not from room geometry — this plate is generative and is not dimensionally consistent (solving its shower head and valve heights together puts the floor at 115% of frame).
_anchor_sizing: Solve unitPerIn = targetWidthFraction * plateAspect / (sizeIn * PHOTO_FRAME_RATIO * contentFraction), where plateAspect is 784/336 = 2.3333 and targetWidthFraction is the product's wanted width as a fraction of plate WIDTH. contentFraction is the share of the catalog frame the product actually fills, and it is the term that matters: scripts/measure-fixtures.mjs finds these three shots filling 94-100% of their frame, NOT the 1/1.5 that PHOTO_FRAME_RATIO assumes, so every overlay drew about 1.5x too large until this was measured rather than trusted. PHOTO_FRAME_RATIO is left at 1.5 because the Three.js plate's anchors were tuned around it and changing it would silently resize the fallback; it is divided back out here instead. Re-run measure-fixtures.mjs if the catalogue's crop ever changes. sizeIn is whatever the caller resolves from the component catalogue — 6in shower head, 6.5in trim, 8.9in faucet.

faucet._covers: baked-in x 54.9-60.0, y 47.9-55.5 (40 x 26 px). Drawn 7.0% of plate width.
faucet._y_note: Centred on 50.3 rather than on the fixture's own centre so the faucet STANDS on the counter. Its photo fills the frame's full width but only 63.5% of its height, centred, so the product's base falls 31.8% of the frame below the anchor — 5.2% of plate height at this scale. The counter's top edge under the faucet is y=55.5, hence 55.5 - 5.2.

showerTrim._covers: baked-in x 20.3-24.3, y 46.5-56.2 (31 x 33 px). Drawn 4.5% of plate width.

showerHead._covers: baked-in x 30.6-35.0, y 6.7-16.0 (35 x 31 px). Drawn 5.5% of plate width.

tubSpout._covers: nothing — this plate has a walk-in shower, no tub. Callers only pin a spout when the dealer picked a tub path, which this plate cannot depict; the anchor exists to satisfy the AnchorId union and puts the spout somewhere plausible rather than at 0,0.

_vanity_junction_note: Both cabinet ends measured by darkest-column search, and they are hard lines, not fades. LEFT: the reveal between the partition face and the cabinet side sits at x=46.94 and does not move between y=59 and y=86 — dead vertical — deepening from 47% to 88% below its shoulders as it descends into shadow. The profile at y=70 runs partition face 194 at x=46.5, then a genuine dark gap of 38-96 from 46.7 to 47.6, then cabinet 177 from 47.9. That gap is REAL geometry photographed in the plate, not a rendering artifact, so the cabinet region now stops at its true edge of 47.85 and the gap is left as plate. RIGHT: the cabinet ends at x=70.70 with its junction line at 70.75 (lum 31-34, depth ~0.70, constant y=62-74). The region previously stopped at 70.00, which left 0.7% of plate width of un-tinted cabinet standing between the composited colour and the wall — that is the gap the markup circled. Contact seams at both lines firm up the read after tinting; they are deliberately light because the plate's own junction shadows are already deep and multiply carries them through.
_plate_repairs_note: EMPTY. The old plate's head paint-out is obsolete — its box lands on bare wall in the new plate and would gouge a patch out of it. The new plate needs no repairs unless a survey finds a defect.
_modeled_head_note: Drawn, not photographed, and placed by the same perspective solve as everything else. x=21.30 is the valve escutcheon's centre: a darkest-column search puts the valve's dark mass at x 20.28-24.12, but that span includes the lever reaching right, and the escutcheon disc itself centres on 21.3. The left return's own centre is 20.53, so 'centred on the wall' and 'above the valve' disagree by 0.77% of plate width and, as directed, above the valve wins. y=26.70 is 79in above the pan — the fixture program's real head height, not the 100in the plate's own head sat at — via y = 36.45 + (y_pan - 36.45) * (1 - 79/65.9) evaluated on the return's pan line at that x. unitPerIn is the return's vertical scale there, 0.7443% of image height per inch, so the assembly is sized from the universal head's catalogue dimensions rather than drawn to taste. It comes out smaller than the plate's baked-in head, which is correct: that one was oversized.
_phase2_survey: PHASE 2 measurements, all zoom-verified on the NEW plate before use. PAN: back edge (24.5,87.8)->(44.5,84.5), slope -0.165/%x; front threshold, a hard dark line, (30,94.8)->(44.5,92.3), slope -0.172/%x; curb face runs about 2.3% below that. Left edge is behind the plant so it is extrapolated to x=17.0 along both lines — the polygon is the pan's TRUE outline, not what is unobscured. CABINET: left junction a hard dark line at x=49.5 with the face starting 50.0; right edge at x=77.3 with its own dark line to 77.6; top under the counter shadow at y=59.3; toe line (where the face ends and the recess begins) 87.3 at x=50 falling to 85.8 at x=70; floor begins y=90.0. COUNTER BAND splits in two and the earlier survey read them as one: the BACKSPLASH is the upper band, top (49.4,51.8)->(77.3,52.6), bottom 55.8->55.4; the COUNTER surface plus its nosing runs 55.8->58.2. There is also a RIGHT SIDE SPLASH, a narrow wood strip at x 77.3-78.1 from y 50.6 to 58.2, which the old plate did not have. PAN CORRECTION: the back-edge slope is -0.106/%x fitted across all four measured profile points, not the -0.165 first read off a zoom crop; that error put the top-left corner 1.25% too low and left a strip of untinted pan showing along the wall.
_phase2_deltas: Corrections found by zoom AFTER the regions first landed, logged because every pass so far has produced some. (1) Cabinet left edge 50.0 -> 49.6: the plate's cabinet stile catches light between the junction shadow at 49.3-49.5 and the face, and stopping at 50.0 left that 0.4% as an untinted sliver. (2) Side splash band 50.6-58.2 -> 52.6-55.4: authored from a first reading that made it stand 2% proud of the back splash and read as a tab; it is the same 4in element and meets the back splash on the shared line at x=77.3. (3) Not geometry: the fixtureRegions still hold OLD-plate boxes and were recolouring a patch of the new counter gold — gated off in the compositor until Phase 3 rebuilds them, same reasoning as the occlusion mask.
